title: Bridging the Gulf? Thailand and Cambodia Turn to UNCLOS | Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative
gist: After Thailand terminated MOU 44 in May 2026, Cambodia launched only the second-ever UNCLOS compulsory conciliation over their ~10,000-square-mile overlapping maritime claims in the hydrocarbon-bearing Gulf of Thailand, with opening statements in Singapore on September 15. The parties diverge — Thailand wants boundary delimitation, Cambodia also wants joint development and resource sharing — and success or failure will shape Southeast Asia's leverage against China in the South China Sea.

themes.theme: MOU 44 termination and the Gulf of Thailand OCA

insights.claim: MOU 44, signed in 2001, governed delimitation and joint resource development in a roughly 10,000-square-mile Thai-Cambodian overlapping claims area, but after only five rounds of talks the two sides never agreed on either issue.
insights.so_what: Gulf of Thailand hydrocarbon resources in the OCA have been stranded for 25 years by the dispute.
insights.quote: MOU 44 treated delimitation and joint development as an “indivisible package”
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Thailand has historically awarded oil and gas concessions within the overlapping claims area to companies including Chevron, PTTEP and BG Asia, a Shell subsidiary.
insights.so_what: Any delimitation or joint-development outcome directly affects the value of these companies' dormant OCA concessions.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Thai PM Anutin Charnvirakul, who campaigned on scrapping MOU 44 ahead of the February 2026 election, terminated it on May 5, arguing it produced no progress in 25 years and that talks could proceed under UNCLOS now that Cambodia had ratified it.
insights.so_what: Nationalist domestic politics after 2025 border clashes is driving Thailand's harder maritime stance.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: An average of 57 Thai fishing vessels per month operated in the OCA from September 2025 to September 2026 per Starboard AIS data; Cambodian vessels went undetected largely because they lack AIS, and Cambodia holds an EU IUU-fishing red card.
insights.so_what: Unregulated fishing activity in the OCA is a potential flashpoint while the dispute is unresolved.
insights.locator: Thailand and Cambodia have never agreed
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Thailand's 2011 Article 298 declaration excludes maritime delimitation from binding procedures; Cambodia withdrew its similar exclusion on May 26, weeks after MOU 44's termination, but binding settlement still requires Thailand's consent.
insights.so_what: Cambodia is signaling readiness for binding arbitration; Thailand retains a veto, limiting any forced outcome.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The five-member commission — Cambodia's appointees Peter Taksøe-Jensen and Jean-Marc Thouvenin, Thailand's former ITLOS presidents Rüdiger Wolfrum and Albert Hoffmann, chaired by Australian Katrina Cooper — must report within 12 months, after which parties must negotiate on the report's basis.
insights.so_what: A roughly 12-month timeline gives a window for a recommendation on boundaries and resource sharing by around mid/late 2027.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The commission has scheduled six more meetings, the next from October 14 to 18 at The Hague; proceedings are confidential by default and non-binding to reduce friction.
insights.so_what: Limited public visibility on progress; watch meeting outcomes for signals.
insights.locator: Compulsory conciliation is intended to foster
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Timor Sea precedent and diverging aims

insights.claim: The only prior UNCLOS compulsory conciliation, Timor-Leste v. Australia from 2016, succeeded: it led to the 2018 Maritime Boundary Treaty, in force from 2019, which set permanent boundaries and a joint-development and revenue-sharing regime for the Greater Sunrise gas field.
insights.so_what: Precedent suggests conciliation can unlock contested offshore gas resources via joint-development regimes.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Unlike Timor Sea, where conciliation helped replace an existing resource-sharing arrangement, the Thai-Cambodian case began with termination of the framework, and the parties diverge: Thailand focuses on boundary delimitation while Cambodia seeks a single boundary plus interim joint development and equitable resource sharing.
insights.so_what: Divergent objectives lower odds of a quick resource-development deal in the Gulf of Thailand.
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Regional implications for South China Sea

insights.claim: Success would reinforce Southeast Asian adherence to international maritime law and legitimize UNCLOS compulsory mechanisms, strengthening regional negotiating positions vis-à-vis China; breakdown or non-compliance could deepen intra-ASEAN fissures on maritime issues.
insights.so_what: The case is a bellwether for rules-based resolution of South China Sea disputes.
insights.quote: which would in turn strengthen their negotiating positions vis-à-vis China in the South China Sea

insights.claim: A December ceasefire paused major armed conflict on the Thai-Cambodian land border after deadly 2025 clashes, but tensions remain high.
insights.so_what: Residual conflict risk in mainland Southeast Asia persists despite legal track.
